content.title: ‘The Fall-Off’ Review: J. Cole’s Sprawling Farewell
content.text: By Mark RichardsonJ. Cole sits in a unique place in the constellation of hip-hop superstars. He’s a rapper’s rapper, someone who prides himself on verbal technique and clarity of expression. And yet his approach to his craft is unusually earnest, devoid of the mystique that surrounds Kendrick Lamar or the mercenary commercial instincts of Drake, to name two of his peers. While the rapper born Jermaine Lamarr Cole and raised in Fayetteville, N.C., has participated in his share of public beefs, he has never acted like he had all the answers. His musical bona fides are undeniable—along with his rapping prowess, he’s also a skilled producer—but he has an everyman quality rare for his genre.Since his 2007 mixtape debut “The Come Up,” Mr. Cole has built a business empire outside of his musical ventures. He has an ownership stake in the NBA’s Charlotte Hornets as well as the music streaming service Tidal, and each of his six studio records has hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 album chart. But as a keen student of the hip-hop game, he knows the difficulty of being a rapper entering middle age: Hip-hop draws its energy from youth culture, and he just turned 41 years old. His seventh LP, “The Fall-Off” (Dreamville/Interscope), out now, is being described as his last.Copyright ©2026 Dow Jones & Company, Inc.
